_meta: A 1-D step edge (0 to 255) resampled with cubic (Catmull-Rom) and with linear interpolation, used to show why cubic/bicubic interpolation OVERSHOOTS the range of its samples at a sharp edge -- producing ringing (halos) and out-of-range values that must be clamped -- while linear interpolation never does. Upscaling an image interpolates new samples between the known pixels. Linear (bilinear in 2-D) interpolation takes a convex combination of the two nearest samples, so every interpolated value lies between them and the result is soft but safe -- it can never leave the range of the surrounding pixels. Cubic (bicubic, Catmull-Rom, Lanczos) interpolation fits a higher-order curve through more neighbors to get a sharper, more detailed result, and that extra sharpness comes from a kernel with negative lobes. Those negative lobes let the fitted curve overshoot: near a high-contrast edge the interpolated values swing BELOW the darker sample and ABOVE the brighter one, a ringing or halo band around the edge, and the overshoot can push pixel values outside the valid range (below 0 or above 255), which then have to be clamped. The overshoot is inherent to the sharper kernel, not a bug -- it is the visible cost of the sharpness, and clamping removes the out-of-range values but not the ring. samples is the step-edge signal; the interpolation is evaluated at fractional positions between samples. samples is the fixture; the cubic and linear interpolated values, their ranges, and the overshoot are computed.
